summary.text: A decimal-digit induction proves that whenever \(x+y=10^k-1\), both \(s(x)+s(y)\) and \(s(5x)+s(5y)\) equal \(9k\), so the corresponding digit-sum differences are negatives and their signs cancel. Pairing the terms in the intervening interval by this complementation makes its total increment zero, yielding the required equality of the two partial sums.

full_proof.text:
Let \(S(n)\) denote the sum of the decimal digits of the nonnegative integer \(n\), with \(S(0)=0\). Define
\[
D(n)=S(5n)-S(n),\qquad \delta(n)=\operatorname{sign}(D(n))\in\{-1,0,1\}.
\]
Thus, if
\[
B(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\delta(j),
\]
then the sequence in the statement is \(a(n)=B(n)\) (in the given definition the integer sum is converted to a natural number, but below we prove equality of the integer sums themselves, so that conversion does not affect the argument).

We will prove that for every \(k>0\), writing
\[
N=10^k,\qquad m=\frac N2-1,
\]
one has
\[
B(m-i)=B(m+i)\qquad(0\le i\le m).
\]

We first establish the digit-sum identities needed for the proof.

For any nonnegative integers \(a,b\) with \(0\le b<10\), the decimal expansion gives
\[
S(10a+b)=S(a)+b. \tag{1}
\]
This is also valid when \(a=b=0\), under the convention \(S(0)=0\).

A useful consequence is that, whenever \(0\le c\le4\),
\[
S(5q+c)=S(5q)+c. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if \(q\) is even, then \(5q\) has last decimal digit \(0\), so adding \(c\le4\) merely changes that last digit from \(0\) to \(c\). If \(q\) is odd, then \(5q\) has last digit \(5\), and adding \(c\le4\) changes it to \(5+c\), again without a carry. More explicitly, writing \(5q=10u+e\), where \(e=0\) if \(q\) is even and \(e=5\) if \(q\) is odd, both \(e\) and \(e+c\) are single decimal digits. Formula (1) therefore gives
\[
S(5q+c)=S(u)+(e+c)=S(u)+e+c=S(5q)+c.
\]

We now prove two complement identities. For every \(k\ge0\) and every \(x<10^k\),
\[
S(x)+S(10^k-1-x)=9k, \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
S(5x)+S\bigl(5(10^k-1-x)\bigr)=9k. \tag{4}
\]

The first identity is the usual decimal-complement identity, but we include a proof. We argue by induction on \(k\). For \(k=0\), the condition \(x<1\) forces \(x=0\), and both digit sums are zero. Suppose (3) is known for \(k\), and let \(x<10^{k+1}\). Write
\[
x=10q+r,\qquad 0\le r\le9.
\]
Then \(q<10^k\), and if
\[
q'=10^k-1-q,\qquad r'=9-r,
\]
we have
\[
10^{k+1}-1-x=10q'+r'.
\]
Using (1) and the induction hypothesis,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(x)+S(10^{k+1}-1-x)
 &=S(q)+r+S(q')+r'\\
 &=9k+9\\
 &=9(k+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (3).

The identity (4) is slightly subtler because multiplication by \(5\) can create carries. Again use induction on \(k\). The case \(k=0\) is immediate, as above. Suppose (4) holds for \(k\), and let
\[
x=10q+r<10^{k+1},\qquad 0\le r\le9.
\]
Set again
\[
q'=10^k-1-q,
\qquad r'=9-r,
\]
so that
\[
10^{k+1}-1-x=10q'+r'.
\]
For any digit \(r\), division into quotient and remainder modulo \(2\) gives
\[
5r=10\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor+5(r\bmod2).
\]
Consequently,
\[
5x=10\left(5q+\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor\right)+5(r\bmod2).
\]
The final term is either \(0\) or \(5\), hence is a decimal digit. Formula (1), followed by (2), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(5x)
 &=S\left(5q+\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor\right)+5(r\bmod2)\\
 &=S(5q)+\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor+5(r\bmod2), \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(0\le\lfloor r/2\rfloor\le4\). The same argument applied to \(r'=9-r\) gives
\[
S\bigl(5(10^{k+1}-1-x)\bigr)
 =S(5q')+\left\lfloor\frac {r'}2\right\rfloor+5(r'\bmod2). \tag{6}
\]

By the induction hypothesis,
\[
S(5q)+S(5q')=9k,
\]
since \(q'=10^k-1-q\). It remains to inspect the contribution from the last digits. Because \(r+r'=9\), exactly one of \(r,r'\) is odd. If the even one is \(2t\), then the odd one is \(9-2t=2(4-t)+1\). Therefore
\[
\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor+5(r\bmod2)
+
\left\lfloor\frac {r'}2\right\rfloor+5(r'\bmod2)
=t+(4-t)+5=9. \tag{7}
\]
Adding (5) and (6), and using (7), now yields
\[
S(5x)+S\bigl(5(10^{k+1}-1-x)\bigr)=9k+9=9(k+1).
\]
Thus (4) holds for every \(k\).

Combining (3) and (4) gives the key antisymmetry of the increments. If \(x<10^k\) and
\[
y=10^k-1-x,
\]
then
\[
S(5x)+S(5y)=9k
\quad\text{and}\quad
S(x)+S(y)=9k.
\]
Subtracting the second equality from the first gives
\[
\bigl(S(5x)-S(x)\bigr)+\bigl(S(5y)-S(y)\bigr)=0,
\]
or equivalently
\[
D(y)=-D(x).
\]
Since \(\operatorname{sign}(-z)=-\operatorname{sign}(z)\), including when \(z=0\), we conclude that
\[
\delta(x)+\delta(y)=0
\qquad\text{whenever }x+y=10^k-1. \tag{8}
\]

We now apply this antisymmetry to the cumulative sums. Fix \(k>0\), put \(N=10^k\), and let
\[
m=\frac N2-1.
\]
Because \(k>0\), \(N\) is even, so
\[
N=2\left(\frac N2\right)
\quad\text{and hence}\quad
2m+1=N-1. \tag{9}
\]
Let \(i\) satisfy \(0\le i\le m\). The terms occurring in \(B(m+i)\) but not in \(B(m-i)\) are exactly those with indices
\[
m-i+1,m-i+2,\ldots,m+i.
\]
There are \(2i\) such terms. Pair them from the two ends: for each \(d=0,1,\ldots,i-1\), define
\[
x_d=m-i+1+d,
\qquad
y_d=m+i-d.
\]
Their sum is
\[
x_d+y_d
=(m-i+1+d)+(m+i-d)
=2m+1
=N-1

the last equality by (9). Moreover, all these indices are nonnegative and less than \(N\). Indeed, the assumption \(i\le m\) gives \(x_d\ge1\), while
\[
y_d\le m+i\le2m=N-2<N.
\]
Thus (8) applies to every pair, and gives
\[
\delta(x_d)+\delta(y_d)=0.
\]
The pairs partition the entire interval from \(m-i+1\) through \(m+i\), so
\[
\sum_{j=m-i+1}^{m+i}\delta(j)
=
\sum_{d=0}^{i-1}\bigl(\delta(x_d)+\delta(y_d)\bigr)
=0. \tag{10}
\]
For \(i=0\), the interval is empty and (10) remains true.

Finally, splitting the cumulative sum at \(m-i\) and using (10),
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(m+i)
&=\sum_{j=0}^{m+i}\delta(j)\\
&=\sum_{j=0}^{m-i}\delta(j)
 +\sum_{j=m-i+1}^{m+i}\delta(j)\\
&=B(m-i).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(a(m-i)=a(m+i)\) for every \(0\le i\le m\), where \(m=10^k/2-1\), as claimed.
